An alias is a name that a person goes by that is not their real, official name. It is an alternative name — a second (or third, or fourth) name that someone uses instead of, or alongside, their true identity.

Think of it this way: every person has one real, legal name. An alias is any other name attached to that same person.

Imagine a criminal named Robert King who doesn't want the police to find him. So when he checks into a hotel, he signs in as "Jack Stone." Jack Stone is his alias — a made-up name he uses to hide who he really is.

This is why you'll often hear aliases mentioned in police reports, courtrooms, and crime dramas. The phrase "also known as" — often shortened to a.k.a. — is almost always a sign that an alias is being introduced.

"Robert King, a.k.a. Jack Stone, was arrested on Tuesday."

Here, Jack Stone is the alias.

There are several very different reasons, and the word "alias" is used across all of them:

1. To hide or deceive
This is the most classic use. A person uses a false name to avoid being identified — by the police, a victim, or anyone else looking for them. This is the context where "alias" carries a slightly suspicious or negative tone.

2. For professional or creative purposes
Many writers, musicians, and performers adopt a name that sounds more appealing, memorable, or marketable than their birth name. These are technically aliases too, though in creative fields people often use softer-sounding words like pen name or stage name instead.

  • The author Samuel Clemens wrote under the alias Mark Twain.
  • The musician Stefani Germanotta performs under the alias Lady Gaga.

3. For privacy or personal preference
Some people simply don't want to use their real name in certain situations — online forums, social media, or communities where they prefer anonymity. The username or handle they choose functions as an alias.

4. In computing and technology
In tech, an alias is a shortcut name that points to something else. For example, an email alias is a secondary email address that quietly redirects all incoming messages to a real inbox. The alias address exists and works, but it's just an alternate label for the real one. Similarly, a programmer might create an alias for a long, complex command — a short, easy nickname that triggers the full command when used.
The Key Characteristics of an Alias

No matter the context, an alias always has these features:

  • It is not the original, official name. The alias is always the secondary name, not the primary one.
  • The person behind it remains the same. An alias changes the name, not the individual. Robert King is still Robert King even when he calls himself Jack Stone.
  • It can be self-chosen or given by others. A criminal might choose their own alias, but investigators might also assign a codename or nickname to a suspect — that too counts as an alias.
  • It may or may not be meant to deceive. A stage name is an alias without dishonest intent. A fake name used to evade the law is an alias with clear deceptive intent. The word "alias" covers both.

Because alias is close in meaning to several other words, it helps to know exactly where it sits:

  • Nickname — A casual, affectionate, or descriptive name given to someone (e.g., "Shorty," "Big Red"). A nickname is usually not meant to replace or hide the real name. Aliases can serve this purpose.
  • Pseudonym — A false name adopted specifically for professional or published work (writing, art, performance). A pseudonym is essentially a type of alias, but used in a more specific, creative context. All pseudonyms are aliases, but not all aliases are pseudonyms.
  • Pen name / Stage name — These are even more specific types of pseudonyms (and therefore aliases), used strictly by writers and performers respectively.
  • Codename — A name assigned (usually by an organization) to a person or operation for secrecy. Also a specific type of alias.

So "alias" is the broadest of these terms. It is the umbrella word that can refer to any of the above in the right context.
Whenever you see or hear the word alias, just ask yourself: "Is this the real name, or a stand-in name for the real one?" If it's a stand-in — for any reason, in any field — it's an alias.
